column3: The binding site is a hollow or cleft on the surface. Swap-trap: an active site does chemistry, a binding site does not.
Two things in one sentence: the bonds are intermolecular (non-covalent) and the result is induced fit, not lock-and-key.
Signal transduction is the downstream domino effect. The signal gets inside the cell; the ligand itself does not have to.
Binding is reversible and the ligand leaves unchanged. A statement saying it is permanently bound or chemically altered is false.
Individually weak, collectively strong. Watch for a flipped version saying they are individually strong.
Specifically induced dipole - induced dipole (van der Waals) in hydrophobic regions, maximized by surface complementarity.
Water can bridge an H-bond that would otherwise be out of reach. It is not always a spectator.
Solvation and desolvation regulate affinity. Expect this as a fill-in or true/false.
Releasing ordered water from a hydrophobic interface is an ENTROPY gain. If a choice credits enthalpy only, it is wrong.
Memorize the three consequences in order: false positives for sensors, high background for imaging, side effects for drugs.
Antibody = immunoglobulin. One word, easy point.
Five classes: IgG, IgM, IgA, IgD, IgE. Remember GAMED. A sixth invented class is the usual distractor.
Antigen binding is set by the VARIABLE region sequence. Constant-region is the swap-trap.
Two functions: bind antigen, and recruit effector cells. The second one is the Fc tail.
Variability is concentrated in the CDRs, not spread evenly. CDR = complementarity determining region.
Circular, replicates in a host, transferable. The parenthesis is the real point: it only replicates if its ori suits that host.
Shuttle = works in TWO organisms. Grow it in bacteria, use it in yeast or human cells.
Cloning vector: purpose is copies of the DNA. Nothing about making protein.
Expression vector: makes mRNA, so it needs a promoter to start and a terminator to stop. Promoter/terminator swap is the classic trap.
RNA synthesis starts at the END of the promoter, which sits 5' of the gene. The promoter is not transcribed itself.
Elongation runs until the terminator, where polymerase releases both the RNA and the DNA template.
Regulatory sequences plus the proteins that bind them switch genes on or off. True in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes.
Three genes; lacZ makes beta-galactosidase; it hydrolyses lactose into glucose + galactose. Know which product is which.
The four-way table. ON only when glucose is ABSENT and lactose is PRESENT. The other three give little to no enzyme.
Proofreading removes the wrong base immediately after it is added. More accurate but slower.
Chromosome level: deletion, inversion, translocation, duplication. Gene level adds substitution and frameshift, so a question mixing the two lists is a trap.
Taq survives the ~94 C denaturation step. That is the whole reason it is used.
Accept the professor's wording. In practice most qPCR uses a dye or a labelled probe; the key idea is fluorescence read every cycle, and an earlier Ct means more starting template.
MCS = many restriction sites clustered in one place, so you get a choice of enzymes.
WHITE = recombinant (insert disrupted lacZ, no beta-gal, X-Gal stays colourless). Blue = empty vector. Getting this backwards is the single most common error here.
Directional cloning needs TWO DIFFERENT enzymes used on both vector and insert, so the insert can only drop in one way round.
Three parts required: promoter, ribosome binding site, terminator. And it must be cDNA, because E. coli cannot splice out introns.
Billions of peptides displayed on phage, then screened for affinity or activity. This is the setup for panning.
Chemical genetics = using a small molecule to change what one gene product does.
FORWARD = phenotype first, then find the protein. Goal: target IDENTIFICATION.
REVERSE = protein first, then find compounds that bind it. Goal: target function and VALIDATION. Forward/reverse swap is a guaranteed trap.
Epigenetics changes expression without changing sequence, and can persist across generations.
Histones are positively charged; acetylation lowers that charge and loosens the DNA grip.
A nucleosome is DNA around 2 copies each of 4 histones. The OCTAMER is the core as a whole, not a single histone, despite the review's wording.
Euchromatin is loose, so RNA polymerase can get in and transcribe.
Heterochromatin is tightly wrapped and inactive. Euchromatin/heterochromatin swap is a frequent trap.
Most of the genome sits in heterochromatin. Counter-intuitive, so it gets asked.
Post-translational modification of histone TAILS sets the packing state.
About 30 amino acids, N-terminal, unstructured, heavily modified, and a docking signal for other proteins.
Methylation does two things: blocks transcription factors AND recruits MBD proteins. Expect a question that only credits one.
Methylation lets the environment tune expression fast, without permanent mutation. This is the agouti mouse and royal jelly story.
CpG dinucleotides, cytosine methylated on BOTH strands, as 5-methylcytosine. Enzyme is DNMT, methyl donor is SAM.
HAT ADDS acetyl, loosens DNA, ACTIVATES. Say it as: HAT adds, so the gene is on.
HDAC REMOVES acetyl, restores positive charge, tightens, REPRESSES. HAT/HDAC reversal is the most likely epigenetics trap on the exam.
Viruses are called non-living because they have no independent metabolism, yet they still evolve and replicate inside hosts.
M13 is filamentous and NON-LYTIC: it slows the cell but does not kill it. That is why phage display works.
Adding genes can change a target phenotype. Pairs with the six strategies short answer.
Selection kills what you do not want; screening lets everything grow and you look. Both are used to find improved mutants.
